Registrations for the 2019 Summer School on spatial and spatiotemporal
computing: processing large-scale Earth observation (University of
Münster, Sept 1–7, 2019) are now open. For more info see:

https://opengeohub.org/summer_school_2019

Registration deadline: 15th of February 2019 24:00 CET.

This summer school is limited to 65 participants. In the case of higher
number of applications invitations candidates will be selected based on
a ranking system, which is based on: solidarity, academic output and
contributions to the open source projects. To remove geographical bias,
participants coming from more distant areas have a priority on the
rankings list.

Lecturers:
- Edzer Pebesma: Analyzing large amounts of Earth Observation data with
R and openEO
- Roger Bivand: Not just R-spatial: sustaining open source geospatial
software stacks / Data, data everywhere, nor any drop to analyse
(without making brave assumptions about how the data represent
underlying processes)
- Michael Sumner: Computer graphics data structures for geo-spatial /
Building a data library and R toolkit for domain-specific research group
/ Challenges of working with data in polar regions
- Markus Neteler: Cloud based processing of geo and Earth observation
data / Introduction to GRASS GIS / Advanced data analysis in GRASS GIS
- Veronica Andreo: Analysis of space-time satellite data for disease
ecology applications with GRASS GIS and R stats / Analyzing space-time
satellite data with GRASS GIS for environmental monitoring
- Martijn Tennekes: Creating thematic maps in R (tmap package)
- Tomislav Hengl: Computing with large rasters in R: introduction to
tiling and parallelization / Spatial and Spatiotemporal prediction using
ensemble Machine Learning
- Hanna Meyer: Machine learning strategies for spatio-temporal data
- Anita Graser: Analyzing movement data
- Madlene Nussbaum: Mastering machine learning for spatial prediction -
overview and introduction in methods / model selection and
interpretation, uncertainty
- Meng Lu: Assessment of global air pollution exposure

Dates:
- February 15th 2019 — Registration deadline;
- Mid March 2019 — All invitation letters send to applicants;
- May 15th 2019 — Deadline for settling registration fees (working
programme confirmed);
- July 15th 2019 — Final programme, data sets and exercises published;
- Sun 1st September to Sun 8th September 2019 (arrival Sunday, departure
Sunday; 7 night accommodation) Summer School;

Note: OpenGeoHub Summer school will be held week after the FOSS4G
conference (Bucharest, 26–30 August 2019).

Registration fees:
The registrations fees for this Summer School will be in the range
400–500 EUR. Registration fees cover costs of using facilities, lunch
and coffee breaks, administration costs, local travel costs, and costs
of travel and accommodation for lecturers. Participants from ODA
countries (employed by an organization or company in ODA-listed country;
http://www.oecd.org/dac/stats/daclist.htm) typically receive a
subsidized price for the registration costs. Also, full-time students
(MSc or PhD level) are offered subsidized price, provided that they are,
at the moment of application, not employed at any University or research
institute.

Here's some suggested next debugging steps. Some may seem trivial, but you wouldn't believe the number of times the mistakes have been very simple oversights.

1. Remove all the bells and whistles to the plot. Create a plot, add the points. If that works, then add the next layer for error bars, then keep adding layers until it breaks. That'll help you find the problem.
2. Double check that indeed season is a variable on the data set, and R thinks it's a factor variable with only 3 levels, AND that those levels are EXACTLY "spring", "summer" and "winter. (in that order).

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'm using the following code to annotate a regression equation on my plot:

lm_eqn <- function(yield_nup){
  # browser()
  m <- segmented.mod
  a <- coef(m)[1]
  a <- ifelse(sign(a) >= 0,
              paste0(" + ", format(a, digits = 4)),
              paste0(" - ", format(-a, digits = 4))  )
  eq1 <- substitute( paste( italic(y) == b, italic(x), a ),
                     list(a = a,
                          b = format(coef(m)[2], digits = 4)))
  eq2 <- substitute( paste( italic(r)^2 == r2 ),
                     list(r2 = format(summary(m)$r.squared, digits = 3)))
  c( as.character(as.expression(eq1)), as.character(as.expression(eq2)))
}

I've tried making alterations to the code, but to no avail. Couldn't seem to find the solution on stack overflow either. I imagine it's a minor tweak, but I can't seem to figure it out for the life of me.

Help anyone??

messages.body_plain:
This isn't a very elegant solution, but assuming you have one rectangle per layer and not many, you could just plot them with plot(rasterstack). You could subset and plot a few at a time with plot(rasterstack)[1:25], etc.  It would be quick to scan for which one does not align (unless it's very subtle) and it's good practice to check all your layers this way anyway. I know you said there are over 1000 and this probably seems really tedious but you may spend more time trying to solve it a fancy way and may miss other issues with your rasters by not plotting them. May even try plotting the subsets in a loop and writing it to a pdf. As an aside I like to do with histograms when working with hundreds of predictor variables so I can refer to it later.

messages.body_plain:
How fun!

+1 for plotting. I’m not sure I see the next step in Scott’s solution, but I’d be curious to hear it if someone thinks of it!

I decided to keep everything spatial, because there are a lot of edge cases if we can’t make any assumptions about how big each rectangle is or how all of the other rectangles might overlap with each other.

My approach is to:
1) Sum all the layers in the stack using calc(). Now the value in each cell represents the number of overlapping rectangles there. You know that your non-overlapping rectangle will be somewhere in the resulting summed raster with cell values of 1 (because there’d only be 1 overlapping layer at those points). It’s possible that there will be other values of 1 if another rectangle overlaps some with your rectangle (meaning it can’t be the rectangle you’re looking for) but also spills over into area not covered by any other rectangle.
2) Convert your summed raster layer into a polygon such that adjacent cells with a value of 1 become a single polygon
3) Turn your raster stack into a list, and iterate over it using your favorite method (I chose lapply())
4) In each iteration, convert that layer’s rectangle to a polygon
5) There will only be *one* layer (the one you’re after) that produces a polygon that fits entirely within the polygon you created in step 2. I used st_within() to test each layer’s polygon against the polygon derived in step 2
6) Use which() on the resulting vector of TRUE’s and FALSE’s to see which layer is non-overlapping with any other!

# Make some data
r1 <- r2 <- r3 <- raster(matrix(0, nrow = 100, ncol = 100))

r1[46:55, 46:55] <- 1
r2[1:10, 1:10] <- 1
r3[41:50, 41:50] <- 1
r4 <- r1

# stack the data
s <- stack(r1, r2, r3, r4)

# plot the data
plot(s)

# sum the layers
s_sum <- calc(s, sum)
plot(s_sum)

# convert the pixels indicating only 1 overlapping rectangle into polygons
sum_poly <- rasterToPolygons(s_sum, function(x) x == 1, dissolve = TRUE) %>% st_as_sf()

# Iterate over the layers in the stack, converting each rectangle to a polygon and seeing whether it fits entirely within the summed polygon
non_overlapping <-
  sapply(as.list(s), FUN = function(r) {
  poly <- rasterToPolygons(r, function(x) x == 1, dissolve = TRUE) %>% st_as_sf()

  st_within(poly, sum_poly, sparse = FALSE)
})

# which layer did it?
which(non_overlapping)

Ooh, lots of interesting ideas here.

I ended up doing something similar to Michael's suggestion, but keeping them in raster format. "master" is the raster with the summed values (e.g. "1" meant only one rectangle claimed that cell, "3" meant 3 rectangles claimed that cell), dta was the original data.frame I used to create the rasters in the first place with the startx/starty as the starting coordinates and sizex/sizey as the length of the rectangle edges.

This saved me from having to do a double for loop for the comparisons and was acceptably fast.

for (i in 1:nrow(dta)){

temp <-raster(nrows=1000,ncols=1000,crs=NA)
vals <- rep(0,ncell(temp))
values(temp) <- vals
rw <- dta[i,]
#get the master values at the rectangle location
out <- master[rw$startx:(rw$startx+rw$sizex-1),rw$starty:(rw$starty+rw$sizey-1)]
#if they all equal 1, that's the winner
if(length(unique(out)) == 1 & unique(out) == 1){
print(i)
break
}
}

As a side note, the Advent of Code has been super fun. Highly recommended if you like solving programming puzzles.

Thanks,
Erica

Nice work, that seems like a good solution to me!  For those of you who were curious, this an example of how it can work outside of a R spatial library.  By the way, this is part II of day 3 in the adventofcode.com <http://adventofcode.com> challenge.  You have to solve the first part to get to the second part

total_area_by_patch <- colSums(df_3) #df_3 is the matrix representing all rasters.  Each row represents one raster.  Each column represents a cell in the stack.
intersections <- rowSums(df_3)
intersections[intersections==1] <- 0 #no intersection gets coded with 0
intersections[intersections>1] <- 2 #all intersections get coded with 2
results <- apply(df_3, 2, function(x) {
  result <- x + intersections
  result[result==2] <- 0
  sum(result)
  })
final_result <- total_area_by_patch - results
which(final_result==0) #this identifies which of the 1,305 rectangles had no intersections, because the value in total area_by_patch and final_result should be exactly the same

> > > > How fun!
> > > >
> > > > +1 for plotting. I’m not sure I see the next step in Scott’s solution, but I’d be curious to hear it if someone thinks of it!
> > > >
> > > > I decided to keep everything spatial, because there are a lot of edge cases if we can’t make any assumptions about how big each rectangle is or how all of the other rectangles might overlap with each other.
> > > >
> > > > My approach is to:
> > > > 1) Sum all the layers in the stack using calc(). Now the value in each cell represents the number of overlapping rectangles there. You know that your non-overlapping rectangle will be somewhere in the resulting summed raster with cell values of 1 (because there’d only be 1 overlapping layer at those points). It’s possible that there will be other values of 1 if another rectangle overlaps some with your rectangle (meaning it can’t be the rectangle you’re looking for) but also spills over into area not covered by any other rectangle.
> > > > 2) Convert your summed raster layer into a polygon such that adjacent cells with a value of 1 become a single polygon
> > > > 3) Turn your raster stack into a list, and iterate over it using your favorite method (I chose lapply())
> > > > 4) In each iteration, convert that layer’s rectangle to a polygon
> > > > 5) There will only be *one* layer (the one you’re after) that produces a polygon that fits entirely within the polygon you created in step 2. I used st_within() to test each layer’s polygon against the polygon derived in step 2
> > > > 6) Use which() on the resulting vector of TRUE’s and FALSE’s to see which layer is non-overlapping with any other!

> > > > # Make some data
> > > > r1 <- r2 <- r3 <- raster(matrix(0, nrow = 100, ncol = 100))
> > > >

> > > > r2[1:10, 1:10] <- 1

> > > >
> > > > # stack the data

> > > >
> > > > # plot the data

> > > >
> > > > # sum the layers

> > > >
> > > > # convert the pixels indicating only 1 overlapping rectangle into polygons
> > > > sum_poly <- rasterToPolygons(s_sum, function(x) x == 1, dissolve = TRUE) %>% st_as_sf()

> > > > # Iterate over the layers in the stack, converting each rectangle to a polygon and seeing whether it fits entirely within the summed polygon
> > > > non_overlapping <-
> > > >   sapply(as.list(s), FUN = function(r) {
> > > >   poly <- rasterToPolygons(r, function(x) x == 1, dissolve = TRUE) %>% st_as_sf()
> > > >
> > > >   st_within(poly, sum_poly, sparse = FALSE)
> > > > })
> > > >
> > > > # which layer did it?
> > > > which(non_overlapping)
> > > >

data and discuss high level concept problems (what is metagenome
assembly?) and low level coding problems (what does this error message
even mean?!) and everything in between. There is no scheduled or
specific activity: people show up with questions about how to analyze
their data, or maybe they are willing to help others. We typically get
questions about experimental design for
transcriptomic/metagenomic/genomic projects, or how to install
software, or how to run their analysis on clusters or the cloud.

Cheers,
Luiz Irber

You may want to look at the approx() function: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/approxfun.html
If you give it a set of x and y points, where x is your weekly time-points and y is your weekly measurements, you can get the linear interpolation for any other time points in-between that you'd like by specifying xout.
I noticed you have a 'Date' column; I don't work a lot with date formats in R, but you *may* need to convert this to just an integer 'days' column (e.g. days since start of experiment) for approx() to work. Hope this helps!
Cheers,
Erin

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: interpolation
messages.body_plain:
Here's a tidyverse-style solution:

library(tidyverse)

# Generate some fake data
dat_weekly <- crossing(
  Date = seq.Date(from = as.Date("2018-01-01"),
                  to = as.Date("2018-04-01"),
                  by = 7),
  site = c("A", "B", "C")) %>%
  mutate(no3 = rnorm(n()))

head(dat_weekly)
#> # A tibble: 6 x 3
#>   Date       site      no3
#>   <date>     <chr>   <dbl>
#> 1 2018-01-01 A      0.825
#> 2 2018-01-01 B     -0.0145
#> 3 2018-01-01 C      0.441
#> 4 2018-01-08 A     -0.149
#> 5 2018-01-08 B     -0.326
#> 6 2018-01-08 C      0.0660

dat_daily <- dat_weekly %>%
  group_by(site) %>%         # Break up the data by site
  summarize(interpolated = list(data_frame(   # For each site, make a data frame
    days = seq.Date(
      from = min(Date),         # with a sequence of days
      to = max(Date),
      by = 1),
    no_interp = approx(        # and use the approx() function to interpolate
      x = Date,                # based on the weekly data
      y = no3,                 # on the new daily sequence
      xout = days)$y)          # and extract only the outcome
  )) %>%
  unnest(interpolated)        # Take each data frame and expand into one big one

head(dat_daily)
#> # A tibble: 6 x 3
#>   site  days       no_interp
#>   <chr> <date>         <dbl>
#> 1 A     2018-01-01     0.825
#> 2 A     2018-01-02     0.686
#> 3 A     2018-01-03     0.547
#> 4 A     2018-01-04     0.408
#> 5 A     2018-01-05     0.269
#> 6 A     2018-01-06     0.130

# How does it look?
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = dat_weekly, mapping = aes(x = Date, y = no3), size = 1.5) +
  geom_point(data = dat_daily, mapping = aes(x = days, y = no_interp), size = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~site, ncol = 1)

Hmm, you shouldn't. Modifying Noam's code to pull in your data (and using only the tidyverse) resulted in the output attached.

library(tidyverse)

# Pull in real data
dat_weekly <- read.csv("../../../Desktop/week.csv") %>%
  mutate(Date = as.Date(Date))

head(dat_weekly)

dat_daily <- dat_weekly %>%
  group_by(site) %>%         # Break up the data by site
  summarize(interpolated = list(data_frame(   # For each site, make a data frame
    days = seq.Date(
      from = min(Date),         # with a sequence of days
      to = max(Date),
      by = 1),
    no_interp = approx(        # and use the approx() function to interpolate
      x = Date,                # based on the weekly data
      y = no3,                 # on the new daily sequence
      xout = days)$y)          # and extract only the outcome
  )) %>%
  unnest(interpolated)        # Take each data frame and expand into one big one

head(dat_daily)

# How does it look?
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = dat_weekly, mapping = aes(x = Date, y = no3), size = 1.5) +
  geom_point(data = dat_daily, mapping = aes(x = days, y = no_interp), size = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~site, ncol = 1)

Note this real data does reveal that the measurements aren't strictly weekly by site. For example, you've got observations for site 1 on May 22, 23, 24, and 25. But it doesn't matter for the interpolation.
